Alibaba Group Holding Limited (Alibaba) — one of China’s largest companies — and its U.S.-based payment processor, AUS Merchant Services Inc. agreed to a $600M non-prosecution agreement July 1 to resolve allegations that they failed to prevent merchants from selling and importing illegal pharmaceuticals, controlled substances, listed chemicals and pill presses into the U.S. 

An ICE @HSI_HQ probe with its @HSTFNCC partners led to Alibaba’s admission that it failed to prevent merchants using its Alibaba(dot)com and AliExpress(dot)com platforms from making about 80,000 product sales, including List I and II chemicals, pharmaceuticals and pharmaceutical counterfeiting equipment.

Alibaba operates one of the world’s largest business-to-business online marketplaces. AUS is a subsidiary of Ant Group, which operates Alipay, one of the largest mobile and digital payment platforms in the world.

Alibaba agreed to pay a criminal monetary penalty of $125 million and to forfeit $200 million. AUS agreed to pay a criminal monetary penalty of $85 million and to forfeit $190 million. 

“This non-prosecution agreement, financial resolution and required compliance reforms makes clear that global e-commerce companies must build systems that prevent the sale and distribution of illegal products before they reach the United States and the U.S. banking system,” said ICE HSI Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon.

tweets.text:
68-year-old Santa Monica man Gregory John Curcio admitted to doxing an ICE attorney by publicly identifying her as an ICE agent, posting her home address and directing others on social media to “swat” her using that address in Feb. 2025.

Swatting is harassment that often involves placing false emergency calls to law enforcement to prompt a significant law enforcement response.

The victim told authorities that Curcio is a former resident at her mother’s apartment building in Santa Monica. She said she never met Curcio, but he had harassed and threatened her mother for years. 

The complaint alleges that Curcio made false allegations and engaged in a campaign to harass the victim and her family beginning from at least January 2024.

Curcio faces a statutory maximum sentence of five years in prison at his Aug. 21 sentencing.

Fidel Ramirez Mancilla’s criminal history includes an incarceration for sexual assault in Santa Clara County, Calif., followed by removal from the United States.

 👉Later, he tried to sneak back into the country, but federal agents caught up with him May 19, 2025. 

👉Then, he was convicted of illegal reentry after removal.

✈️This month, ICE picked him up as he was released from federal prison and deported him home to Mexico again.

👍Thanks to the Trump administration’s firm approach to border security, he can’t harm anyone on American soil ever again.
